title: Ten Moves of Good Habits
idea: No trap, no opponent's plan to refute — just the five habits, one move at a time, with the app measuring whether you are actually following them. There is deliberately more than one right answer at almost every step, because the point is not a move order. The point is that every move you make should take a central square, bring out a new piece, or get your king safe, and you should be able to say which.

cues.text: Centre first: d4, e4, d5 and e5 are worth more than any other squares.
Every piece once, before any piece twice.
The king belongs off e1 by about move eight.

plan.goal: Take a central square, develop a new piece, or castle. Every move.
Have at least two minor pieces out by move five.
Keep the king able to castle — do not walk him or lose the right.

line.threat: Move one. There is no threat — there is only the question of what a good opening move is for.
hints: A good first move takes central squares and opens lines for your pieces.
Two pawn moves do this better than any other. Both are in the middle.
Push a central pawn two squares — e4 is the most direct.

moves.why: Takes a central square and frees two pieces at once. Any move that does both of those things is a good opening move.

then.threat: Both sides have a pawn in the centre. Now it is about pieces.
hints: Develop a piece — and prefer one that also does a job.
Knights before bishops, because you already know where the knight belongs.
Knight to f3, attacking e5 and covering d4.

moves.why: Develops, attacks something, covers a central square, and clears a path to castle. Four jobs in one move — that is what makes it the most played second move in chess.
Black defends and develops in the same move.

hints: Another piece. Which one has a clear best square?
The light-squared bishop, and it wants the diagonal that points at f7.

moves.why: The bishop takes its best diagonal and you are one move from castling.

hints: Three pieces are out. What has not happened yet?
Your king is still in the centre and the position is about to open.

moves.why: King safe, rook connected to the game. Almost every trap in this app's Tier 1 stops working the moment this move is played.
Black develops and prepares to castle in turn.

terminal.summary: Four moves, four habits: a central pawn, a knight, a bishop, and the king to safety. Notice that you never had to calculate anything. If you can do this reliably — and check the metric tiles to see it happening — you will stop losing games in the opening, which is most of what separates you from the players currently beating you.

moves.why: Defends e4 and opens the last minor piece. Fine, as long as castling comes next.
Another piece out, defending e4. Also good — this is a position with several right answers.

mistakes.why: Moving a developed piece a second time to attack f7 before you have castled. Black answers d5 and the knight has to come back, having achieved nothing while your king sits in the centre.
A waiting move while a bishop and a knight are still on their starting squares and your king is in the middle. In the opening, a move that develops nothing is a move given away.

moves.why: The Ruy Lopez — an excellent square, pinning the knight that defends e5.
Striking in the centre immediately. Sharp and completely sound.

mistakes.why: The bishop is now staring at its own unmoved d-pawn, and it blocks that pawn from ever advancing. Never place a piece in front of a pawn you still want to move.
The queen blocks her own bishop on f1. You cannot develop it now without moving the queen a second time, which costs you a move and breaks the rule about moving pieces twice.
A rook's pawn move while two minor pieces are at home and your king is in the centre. It takes no central square, develops nothing, and does not help your king.

moves.why: Develops toward the centre. Perfectly good, though it does not attack anything yet.
A second central pawn, immediately. Sound and aggressive.
The King's Gambit — a real opening and a genuine fight. It breaks the habits deliberately, which is fine once you know what you are giving up. Not what this drill is teaching.

mistakes.why: The Wayward Queen. Everything Black plays from here develops a piece and attacks her, so you spend the opening running away. There is a whole lesson on this in Tier 1.
A knight on the rim touches four squares instead of eight, and it does nothing about the centre. Knights belong on f3 and c3.

moves.why: Equally good. Takes a central square, opens the dark-squared bishop, and leads to quieter positions.
Develop first, decide the pawn structure later. Flexible and completely sound.
The English. It controls d5 from a distance rather than occupying the centre — a different but legitimate way to fight for the same squares.

mistakes.why: A rook's pawn takes no central squares, develops nothing, and weakens the squares around where your king is going to live. Ask of every opening move: centre, piece, or king safety? This is none of the three.
A knight on the rim. From h3 it touches four squares; from f3 it touches eight and attacks the centre.
Same problem as h4 — it does not fight for the centre, it does not develop, and it does not help your king. In the opening that is a move handed to your opponent.

recognition.prompt: White has just played Bd3. Which habit does it break?

choices.text: It blocks a pawn White still wants to move
choices.why: The bishop now stands directly in front of the unmoved d-pawn. That pawn cannot advance without the bishop moving again, so the bishop will spend the game looking at its own pawn. Bc4 does the same job on a diagonal that is actually open.

choices.text: It develops a bishop before a knight
choices.why: Both knights are already out, so that rule is satisfied. The problem is the square, not the order.

choices.text: It brings the queen out early
choices.why: The queen has not moved. This is about the bishop.

choices.text: Nothing — d3 is a normal square for that bishop
choices.why: It is a normal square once the d-pawn has moved. With the pawn still on d2 it is a self-inflicted traffic jam.
